aliases: turn a design into a physical machine
svg to a machine that draws or cuts
summary: Take a 2D graphic design (an SVG vector or a raster image) and turn it into physical motion on a machine you build yourself: software converts the design to G-code toolpaths, open firmware on a microcontroller runs the G-code, and a host app streams it over USB to a 2-axis machine (pen plotter, drag-knife cutter, or light diode laser) assembled from orderable parts.

capabilities.capability: host / G-code sender (streams G-code over USB)

capabilities.query: arduino cnc shield a4988 stepper driver power supply usb

capabilities.capability: motion + frame (steppers, belts, linear motion, structure)
capabilities.query: nema17 stepper gt2 belt linear rod rail extrusion frame

capabilities.capability: tool head + sensors (pen lift or laser, endstops)
capabilities.query: servo pen lift diode laser module endstop limit switch

build_steps.title: Order the parts
build_steps.detail: Use bill-of-materials.md / order-list.csv. The base build is an Arduino Uno + CNC Shield V3 with two A4988 (or DRV8825) drivers, two NEMA17 steppers, GT2 belts and pulleys, linear motion (rods+LM8UU or MGN12 rails), a frame (2020 extrusion or laser-cut/printed), a 12V/24V power supply, endstops, and a tool head (SG90 servo pen lift to start; a diode laser module later).

build_steps.title: Flash the controller firmware
build_steps.detail: Flash GRBL to the Arduino Uno (grbl for ATmega328), or FluidNC to an ESP32 board if you want Wi-Fi and a web UI. Set steps/mm, max rate, and acceleration for your steppers and pulley/belt pitch. GRBL config is the $$ settings; FluidNC uses a config.yaml.

build_steps.title: Assemble the machine
build_steps.detail: Build the frame, mount the two axes (X carriage on Y gantry, or a CoreXY layout), fit belts and pulleys, wire the steppers to the drivers on the CNC shield, wire the endstops, and mount the tool head. Set the A4988 driver current (Vref) before powering the motors.

build_steps.title: Convert your design to G-code
build_steps.detail: For vector art, run svg2gcode (or vpype + vpype-gcode) to turn your SVG paths into G-code with pen-up/pen-down (or laser on/off) moves. For a raster image, use an image-to-gcode tool. Set travel/feed rates and the pen-lift servo angles (or laser PWM S-values).

build_steps.title: Stream and run
build_steps.detail: Open the G-code in a host sender (Universal Gcode Sender, CNCjs, or bCNC), connect over USB serial, home the machine, jog to the work origin, and run the job. Watch the first run closely and keep the power switch in reach.

safety: If you fit a diode laser: it can permanently blind you and start fires. Wear laser-safety goggles rated for the exact wavelength (usually 445nm blue), never run it unattended, enclose the beam, add a fume extractor for cut materials, and keep a fire extinguisher nearby. For the mechanical build, set stepper-driver current correctly to avoid overheating, and disconnect power before touching wiring.
